Class 13 in three facts
  • WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3) replaces the pre-shared-key exchange of WPA2 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 2) with SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals), which resists offline guessing of the Wi-Fi passphrase

Symmetric encryption, asymmetric encryption, hash functions and steganography.

1.1 What cryptography does, and the vocabu…1.2 Symmetric encryption: one shared key1.3 Asymmetric encryption: a key pair1.4 Hybrid encryption: how real systems co…1.5 Hash functions1.6 A brief look at steganographyVideosReal-life exampleCodeVisualizationFlashcardsQuestions

1.1 What cryptography does, and the vocabulary we need

Slide 7What cryptography gives: four security services

  • Cryptography: protecting information with mathematical algorithms, so that only authorized parties can read it and changes or a false origin can be detected
Confidentiality
Only authorized parties can read the information
Integrity
Any change, accidental or deliberate, is detected
Authentication
You can verify who produced the data or who is at the other end
Non-repudiation
A signer cannot credibly deny a signature made with the private key
  • Not provided by cryptography: availability (redundancy, backups, DoS (Denial of Service) defenses, Class 12)

Slide 8Core vocabulary, key space and Kerckhoffs's principle

  • Plaintext: readable data · Ciphertext: the unreadable result
  • Encryption turns plaintext into ciphertext; decryption reverses it
  • Algorithm (cipher): the published procedure · Key: the secret value that makes the result unique
  • Key length: size of the key in bits · Key space: all possible keys = 2^length
  • Kerckhoffs's principle (1883): a system must stay secure even when everything except the key is public
    • Use published, standardized algorithms (AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output), RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman), ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)), never a home-made method
    • Canada: CCCS (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security) ITSP.40.111 lists approved algorithms · United States: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) standards

2¹²⁸ ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸possible values of a 128-bit key

Sources: https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/cryptographic-algorithms-unclassified-protected-protected-b-information-itsp40111 · https://csrc.nist.gov/

1.2 Symmetric encryption: one shared key

Slide 9Symmetric encryption (1/3): one shared key

  • Symmetric encryption: the same secret key encrypts and decrypts: C = E(K, P) and P = D(K, C)
  • Block cipher: works on fixed-size blocks. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard): 128-bit blocks; keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits; 10, 12 or 14 rounds (FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 197)
  • Stream cipher: a keystream combined with the plaintext bit by bit (XOR (exclusive OR)). ChaCha20 (RFC (Request for Comments) 8439), used by WireGuard
  • Retired: DES (Data Encryption Standard) (56-bit key found in 56 hours in 1998) · Triple DES (phased out by the end of 2023)

Plaintext ledger.csv→Encrypt AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) + key K→Ciphertext unreadable→Decrypt AES + same key K→Plaintext ledger.csv

Sources: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/197/final · https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8439 · https://www.eff.org/press/releases/eff-des-cracker-machine-brings-honesty-crypto-debate

Slide 10Symmetric encryption (2/3): modes of operation and the nonce

  • Mode of operation: the rule that applies a block cipher to a whole file; it matters as much as the algorithm
  • Nonce: a number used once (96 bits for GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)). Reusing it with the same key reveals plaintext information and allows forged tags
  • AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data): a mode that gives confidentiality and integrity together (GCM (Galois/Counter Mode), ChaCha20-Poly1305)
ModeHow it worksVerdict
ECB (Electronic Codebook)Each block encrypted alone: identical blocks give identical ciphertextNever use (Figure 4.1)
CBC (Cipher Block Chaining)Each block chained to the previous one; random initialization vectorHides patterns, no integrity
GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)Counter mode + 128-bit authentication tagConfidentiality + integrity
XTS (XEX-based Tweaked-codebook mode with ciphertext Stealing)Designed for disk sectorsBitLocker, disk encryption

Slide 11Symmetric encryption (3/3): the two key problems

  • Strengths: very fast, short keys, ideal for bulk data (disks, VPN (Virtual Private Network) traffic)
  • Key distribution problem: both sides need the same key, delivered through a channel the attacker cannot read
  • Scalability: one key per pair of people = n(n−1)/2 keys
    • NorthMaple, 10 people: 45 keys
    • 100 people: 4,950 keys · 1,000 people: 499,500 keys
  • Asymmetric cryptography needs only 2n keys (next slide)

1.3 Asymmetric encryption: a key pair

Slide 12Asymmetric encryption (1/2): a key pair

  • Asymmetric encryption (public-key cryptography): two mathematically linked keys
  • Public key: given to anyone · Private key: kept secret, never leaves its owner
  • One-way function: easy to compute, infeasible to reverse
  • RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) (1977): factoring large numbers · ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography): elliptic-curve discrete logarithm
  • 256-bit ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography) ≈ 3072-bit RSA (about 128-bit security)
  • n people need 2n keys (NorthMaple: 20); only public keys are distributed
  • Costs: much slower than AES (Advanced Encryption Standard); small data only (RSA-3072 (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman, 3072-bit modulus) with OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding): at most 318 bytes)
  • Who really owns a public key? Certificates and PKI (Public Key Infrastructure), Class 15

Slide 13Asymmetric encryption (2/2): three different uses

1 · Confidentiality
Encrypt with the RECIPIENT'S public key; only her private key decrypts
2 · Digital signature
Sign the hash with the SIGNER'S private key; anyone verifies with the public key: integrity, authentication, non-repudiation
3 · Key agreement
Diffie–Hellman (1976); ECDH (Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman) with X25519: both sides compute the same secret, which never travels (WireGuard, TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3)
  • With RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman), what one key transforms only the other key of the pair reverses
  • Elliptic-curve keys are used for key agreement (ECDH (Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman), X25519) and signatures (ECDSA (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm), Ed25519)

1.4 Hybrid encryption: how real systems combine both

Slide 14Hybrid encryption: how real systems combine both

  • Hybrid encryption combines the strengths of both families:
    • 1. Asymmetric cryptography authenticates and establishes a random session key
    • 2. Symmetric AEAD (AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode), ChaCha20-Poly1305) protects the data
    • 3. A hash or authentication tag protects integrity
  • Used by TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3, SSH (Secure Shell) and WireGuard
  • WireGuard: Curve25519 (ECDH (Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman)), ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s

See Figure 1.4 in the Visualization part of this lesson: the three primitives side by side.

Sources: https://www.wireguard.com/protocol/

1.5 Hash functions

Slide 15Hash functions (1/2): a fixed-size, one-way digest

  • Cryptographic hash function: any input → fixed-size digest; no key, not reversible, not encryption
  • SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output): always 256 bits = 64 hexadecimal characters, for 3 bytes or for 5 GB (gigabyte)
  • Deterministic · preimage resistance (one-way) · second-preimage resistance · collision resistance
  • Avalanche effect: "abc" → ba7816bf…15ad, "abd" → a52d159f…49c9: about half of the bits change

Slide 16Hash functions (2/2): algorithms and where defenders use them

  • Broken for collisions: MD5 (Message Digest 5) (since 2004) and SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) (SHAttered, 2017)
  • Current: SHA-2 (Secure Hash Algorithm 2) (SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output), SHA-384 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 384-bit output), SHA-512 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 512-bit output); FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 180-4) and SHA-3 (Secure Hash Algorithm 3) (FIPS 202)
  • Birthday bound: a collision search needs about 2^(n/2) attempts, so SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) gives about 128-bit collision security
  • Uses: file integrity · digital signatures · password storage (Lesson 2) · HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code) (hash + secret key: integrity and origin)
  • A digest proves integrity only if the reference digest is trusted (Ubuntu signs SHA256SUMS with GPG (GNU Privacy Guard))

Verify a download (Ubuntu tutorial)

$ printf abc | sha256sum
ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223
b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad  -

$ sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
ubuntu-26.04.1-live-server-amd64.iso: OK

Sources: https://shattered.io/ · https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final · https://ubuntu.com/tutorials/how-to-verify-ubuntu · https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104

1.6 A brief look at steganography

Slide 17Steganography: hiding that a message exists

  • Steganography hides the existence of a message; cryptography hides its meaning
  • Cover medium + message → stego object; often encrypt first, then hide
  • LSB (Least Significant Bit) substitution: change the least significant bit of each colour value (±1 out of 255: invisible)
  • Capacity: 800 × 600 pixels × 3 bits = 180,000 bytes
  • Defender view: hidden malware or data exfiltration (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1027.003); detection = steganalysis, DLP (Data Loss Prevention), IDS (Intrusion Detection System)
  • Legitimate use: digital watermarking

Sources: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/003/

Key terms of Lesson 1

Cryptography
The science of protecting information with mathematical algorithms so that only authorized parties can read it and so that modification or false origin can be detected.
Plaintext / ciphertext
Plaintext is readable data; ciphertext is the unreadable result of encryption.
Key / key length / key space
The secret value used by an algorithm; its size in bits; the set of all possible keys (2 to the power of the key length).
Kerckhoffs's principle
A cryptosystem must stay secure even if everything except the key is public; use published, standardized algorithms.
Symmetric encryption
One shared secret key both encrypts and decrypts (AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), ChaCha20). Fast; the key must be distributed securely.
Mode of operation
The rule that applies a block cipher to data longer than one block (ECB (Electronic Codebook), CBC (Cipher Block Chaining), GCM (Galois/Counter Mode), XTS (XEX-based Tweaked-codebook mode with ciphertext Stealing)).
AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) / authentication tag
An encryption mode that provides confidentiality and integrity; the tag detects any modification of the ciphertext.
Nonce
A number used only once with a given key; reuse with GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) leaks information about the plaintexts and allows forged authentication tags.
Asymmetric encryption
Two linked keys: the public key is shared, the private key is kept secret (RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman), ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)).
Digital signature
A value computed from a document's hash with the signer's private key; anyone verifies it with the public key.
Diffie-Hellman key exchange
A method for two parties to compute the same shared secret over an open network without sending it.
Hybrid encryption / session key
Asymmetric cryptography establishes a random symmetric session key; symmetric encryption protects the data.
Hash function / digest
A one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size output; no key, not reversible.
Collision resistance
It is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest.
Avalanche effect
A one-bit change in the input changes about half of the output bits.
HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)
A hash computed with a secret key; proves integrity and origin.
Steganography / LSB (Least Significant Bit) substitution
Hiding the existence of a message inside a cover file, for example in the least significant bits of pixel values.

Real-life example 1 Sending the Q3 client ledger to the remote worker

Slide 19Real-life example 1: sending the Q3 ledger to the remote worker

The task of this example

Encrypt NorthMaple's client ledger so that only the remote worker can read it, deliver the key without ever sending it in clear, and prove that the file arrived unchanged.

How it relates to Lesson 1: The task uses all three primitives of this lesson in one workflow: symmetric encryption (AES-256-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key, Galois/Counter Mode)) for the data, asymmetric encryption (RSA-3072 (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman, 3072-bit modulus) with OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding)) for the key, and a hash function (SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output)) for integrity. It is hybrid encryption, section 1.4.

The situation

NorthMaple Accounting Inc. holds client financial records, which are personal information under PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) and Québec's private-sector privacy act. On Monday, the accountant must send Q3_client_ledger.csv from the file server NM-FS01 to the remote worker on NM-RW01. The remote worker generated her RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) key pair once, on her own machine, and gave the IT (Information Technology) administrator only her public key. The administrator (1) records the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digest of the file, (2) encrypts the file with a fresh AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key) session key in GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) mode, (3) encrypts that session key with the remote worker's public key, and (4) sends the three pieces. On arrival, the remote worker unwraps the key with her private key, decrypts, recomputes the digest and compares. A last test flips one single bit to prove that tampering is detected.

Where it comes back in the course

Today's guided exercise (after the 7:30 pm break): you hash a file with OpenSSL and verify its integrity, which is step (1) and the final comparison of this example. LAB_06, part 1 (Class 16): the remote worker's WireGuard configuration uses the same idea, a private key that stays on NM-RW01 and a public key given to the firewall NM-FW01. LAB_06, part 2 (Class 17): you encrypt company data and validate that the encryption is really in place.

Deliverable you will reuse

An encryption evidence record with four lines: the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digest before sending, the algorithms used (AES-256-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key, Galois/Counter Mode), RSA-3072-OAEP (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman, 3072-bit modulus, Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding)), the SHA-256 digest after receiving with the word MATCH, and the result of the tamper test. Keep the format: the validation section N.4 of Chapter 6 of your Course Procedure Manual asks for exactly this kind of evidence.

Code 1 c14_L1_hybrid_encryption.py

⚠ Lab only (Legal Notice, sections 3 and 4)

Run Code 1 only inside your isolated laboratory, on your own lab machines, never against a system, account or communication that is not yours. The ledger, the keys and the tamper test are created by the script inside your lab machine.

What this code does and how it relates to the lecture

The script performs the whole exchange of Real-life example 1 on one machine: it builds a fictional ledger, records its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digest, creates the remote worker's RSA-3072 (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman, 3072-bit modulus) key pair, encrypts the ledger with a random AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key) key in GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) mode, wraps that key with RSA-OAEP (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman with Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding), decrypts on the receiving side, compares the digests, and finally proves that a single flipped bit is rejected. It illustrates sections 1.2 (symmetric), 1.3 (asymmetric), 1.4 (hybrid) and 1.5 (hash) of the lecture.

Run it in your lab: Ubuntu (NM-LX01 or NM-RW01): sudo apt install python3-cryptography, then python3 c14_L1_hybrid_encryption.py. The keys and the nonce are random, so your digests of the ciphertext differ at every run; the SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) of the ledger stays the same because the ledger text is fixed.
c14_L1_hybrid_encryption.py · Python 3 Step 0
#!/usr/bin/env python3
# =============================================================================
# c14_L1_hybrid_encryption.py      Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) - Class 14
# TASK: Protect the NorthMaple client ledger while it travels from the
#       accountant (file server NM-FS01) to the remote worker (NM-RW01),
#       using the three primitives of Lesson 1 together:
#         - symmetric encryption  (AES-256-GCM)  encrypts the file itself,
#         - asymmetric encryption (RSA-3072 with OAEP padding) protects the AES key,
#         - a hash function       (SHA-256)      proves the file arrived unchanged.
# LAB ONLY: fictional data. Run it inside your isolated lab (NM-LX01 or NM-RW01).
# Needs: Python 3 and the "cryptography" package
#        (Ubuntu: sudo apt install python3-cryptography).
# =============================================================================

# Load the operating-system module: os.urandom() reads the kernel's cryptographically secure random number generator.
import os
# Load Python's built-in hash library; it provides the SHA-256 hash function used for the integrity check.
import hashlib
# Load the RSA key-pair generator (rsa) and the padding schemes (padding) that RSA needs to encrypt safely.
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import rsa, padding
# Load the hash-algorithm objects; the OAEP padding scheme uses SHA-256 internally.
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
# Load AESGCM: the AES block cipher running in Galois/Counter Mode, an authenticated-encryption (AEAD) mode.
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM
# Load InvalidTag: the error that GCM raises when the ciphertext, key, nonce or tag does not verify.
from cryptography.exceptions import InvalidTag

# STEP 1 - Build the fictional ledger as bytes, because encryption and hashing operate on bytes, not on text.
ledger = b"client_id,client_name,balance_cad\nC-1001,Tremblay Renovations,48250.00\nC-1002,Gagnon Dental Clinic,12990.75\n"
# Print the plaintext size; we compare it later with the size of the ciphertext.
print(f"[1] Plaintext ledger: {len(ledger)} bytes")

# STEP 2 - Compute the SHA-256 digest of the original file; this is the reference value for the integrity check.
digest_before = hashlib.sha256(ledger).hexdigest()
# Print the digest: always 64 hexadecimal characters (256 bits), whatever the size of the input.
print(f"[2] SHA-256 before sending: {digest_before}")

# STEP 3 - The remote worker creates an RSA key pair once, on NM-RW01 (public exponent 65537, 3072-bit modulus).
private_key = rsa.generate_private_key(public_exponent=65537, key_size=3072)
# Derive the matching public key from the private key; only this public half is ever given to the accountant.
public_key = private_key.public_key()
# Print the key size; 3072 bits is the RSA size recommended for protection beyond 2030.
print(f"[3] Remote worker key pair created: RSA-{public_key.key_size}")

# STEP 4 - The accountant creates a fresh random 256-bit AES key used for this file only (a session key).
aes_key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)
# Create a random 96-bit (12-byte) nonce; with GCM a nonce must never be reused with the same key.
nonce = os.urandom(12)
# Print only the first 4 bytes of the key: printing a complete key is bad practice, even in a lab.
print(f"[4] AES-256 session key: {aes_key[:4].hex()}... ({len(aes_key) * 8} bits), nonce: {nonce.hex()}")

# STEP 5 - Encrypt the ledger with AES-256-GCM; the result is the ciphertext followed by a 16-byte authentication tag.
ciphertext = AESGCM(aes_key).encrypt(nonce, ledger, None)
# Print the size (plaintext + 16-byte tag) and the first 16 bytes, which look random and reveal nothing.
print(f"[5] Ciphertext: {len(ciphertext)} bytes ({len(ledger)} + 16-byte tag), starts {ciphertext[:16].hex()}")

# STEP 6 - Build the OAEP padding object with SHA-256; OAEP is the recommended padding for RSA encryption.
oaep = padding.OAEP(mgf=padding.MGF1(algorithm=hashes.SHA256()), algorithm=hashes.SHA256(), label=None)
# Encrypt ("wrap") the small AES key with the remote worker's PUBLIC key; only her private key can reverse it.
wrapped_key = public_key.encrypt(aes_key, oaep)
# Print the wrapped-key size: it always equals the RSA modulus size, 3072 bits = 384 bytes.
print(f"[6] AES key wrapped with the RSA public key: {len(wrapped_key)} bytes")

# STEP 7 - Assemble what travels on the network: wrapped key + nonce + ciphertext (no secret travels in clear).
package = {"wrapped_key": wrapped_key, "nonce": nonce, "ciphertext": ciphertext}
# Print the total package size; neither the plaintext nor the AES key appears in it.
print(f"[7] Package sent: {sum(len(part) for part in package.values())} bytes (no plaintext, no readable key)")

# STEP 8 - On NM-RW01: unwrap the AES key with the PRIVATE key; no other key can do this.
recovered_key = private_key.decrypt(package["wrapped_key"], oaep)
# Decrypt and verify in one call: GCM checks the authentication tag before it returns any plaintext.
received = AESGCM(recovered_key).decrypt(package["nonce"], package["ciphertext"], None)
# Recompute the SHA-256 digest of the file that was received.
digest_after = hashlib.sha256(received).hexdigest()
# Compare both digests: identical digests show that the file is bit-for-bit identical to the original.
print(f"[8] SHA-256 after receiving:  {digest_after} -> {'MATCH' if digest_after == digest_before else 'MISMATCH'}")

# STEP 9 - Tamper test: copy the ciphertext into a byte array, a type whose bytes can be modified.
tampered = bytearray(package["ciphertext"])
# Flip one single bit of the first byte (XOR with 1) to imitate an attacker who alters the data in transit.
tampered[0] ^= 0x01
# Open a protected block: if decryption raises an error, Python jumps to the "except" branch below.
try:
    # Decrypt the altered ciphertext with the correct key and nonce; GCM recomputes the tag and compares it.
    AESGCM(recovered_key).decrypt(package["nonce"], bytes(tampered), None)
    # This line runs only if the change was NOT detected; with GCM it never prints.
    print("[9] Tampered data accepted (this should never happen)")
# Catch the integrity failure: the recomputed tag did not match the tag that came with the data.
except InvalidTag:
    # Report the result: one flipped bit is enough for the whole file to be refused.
    print("[9] Tamper test: 1 bit flipped -> InvalidTag -> file REJECTED, nothing decrypted")

    Replay of a real run recorded on September 30, 2026 (Ubuntu, Python 3.11, cryptography 46.0.7, OpenSSL 3.0.13). Keys, salts and nonces are random, so your own run prints different values; the logic and the results are the same.
    Step-by-step explanation
    1. Lines 16–26, imports. os gives access to the operating system's cryptographically secure random generator; hashlib provides SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output); the cryptography package provides RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman), the OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) padding and AES-GCM (Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode). Nothing cryptographic is written by hand: this is Kerckhoffs's principle in practice.
    2. Step 1, the data. The ledger is a byte string of 108 bytes. Encryption and hashing work on bytes, not on characters.
    3. Step 2, the reference digest. hashlib.sha256(ledger).hexdigest() returns 64 hexadecimal characters. This value is written in the evidence record before anything is sent.
    4. Step 3, the key pair. rsa.generate_private_key(65537, 3072) creates the remote worker's private key; .public_key() derives the public half. In real life this happens once, on NM-RW01, and only the public key is handed over.
    5. Step 4, the session key and the nonce. AESGCM.generate_key(256) draws 32 random bytes; os.urandom(12) draws a 96-bit nonce. A new key and a new nonce are created for every file.
    6. Step 5, symmetric encryption. AESGCM(aes_key).encrypt(nonce, ledger, None) returns 124 bytes: 108 bytes of ciphertext plus the 16-byte authentication tag.
    7. Step 6, asymmetric key wrapping. The 32-byte AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key is encrypted with the remote worker's public key using OAEP (Optimal Asymmetric Encryption Padding) padding with SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output). The result always has the size of the RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) modulus: 384 bytes.
    8. Step 7, the package. Wrapped key, nonce and ciphertext travel together (520 bytes). The nonce is not secret; the plaintext and the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key never appear in clear.
    9. Step 8, reception. private_key.decrypt() recovers the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key; AESGCM.decrypt() verifies the tag and returns the plaintext; the new SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digest is compared with the reference. Equal digests print MATCH.
    10. Step 9, tamper test. tampered[0] ^= 0x01 flips the lowest bit of the first ciphertext byte. GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) recomputes the tag, finds a difference and raises InvalidTag; the except branch reports that the file is rejected and that nothing was decrypted.

    Secure storage of credentials: why systems store hashes, and what salting means
    

    

    

    

    Slide 20Secure storage of credentials
    

    Why systems store hashes, and what salting means.
    

    2.1 The problem: verify a password without…2.2 How hash-based verification works2.3 Why a fast, unsalted hash is not enoug…2.4 Salting2.5 Pepper and work factor2.6 Where operating systems keep password …2.7 Verifying safely, and choosing good pa…VideosReal-life exampleCodeVisualizationFlashcardsQuestions
    

    2.1 The problem: verify a password without keeping it
    

    Slide 21The problem: verify a password without keeping it
    • A password is an authentication factor: something you know. The system must keep some reference value to check it
    ✗  Plaintext
    Anyone who reads the database reads every password. rockyou.txt: about 32 million plaintext passwords (2009)
    ✗  Reversible encryption
    The decryption key sits on the same server: steal both and read everything
    ✓  One-way hash
    Store only a hash; the password itself is never kept
    

    2.2 How hash-based verification works
    

    Slide 22How hash-based verification works
    • Enrollment: hash the new password and store the record · Verification: hash the typed password the same way and compare
    • Equal values = correct password. A stolen table gives digests, not passwords
    


    

    2.3 Why a fast, unsalted hash is not enough
    

    Slide 23Why a fast, unsalted hash is not enough
    • Identical passwords → identical digests: reuse is visible to anyone who reads the table
    • Lookup table: precomputed pairs digest → password
    • Rainbow table: compressed chains of hash and reduction steps; trades computing time for storage
    • Both are prepared once and reused against every system with the same unsalted hash
    • Fast by design: under 1 µs per SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) on one core; billions per second on a GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)
    • Windows NT (New Technology) hash = MD4 (Message Digest 4) of the password, not salted (Microsoft) → protect the SAM (Security Account Manager) and Active Directory files
    3 of 4lab passwords recovered instantly by a table lookup in Code 2
    Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/security/kerberos/passwords-technical-overview
    

    2.4 Salting
    

    Slide 24Salting
    • Salt: a unique random value per password, combined with it before hashing, stored in clear next to the hash
    • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology): at least 32 bits; common choice 128 bits (16 bytes)
    • Effect 1: identical passwords → different hashes
    • Effect 2: precomputed tables become useless
    • Effect 3: each account must be attacked separately
    • A salt is not secret and does not make a weak password strong
    Same password, two salts (recorded run of Code 2)
    accountant1  Maple2026!
  salt 14jv57seoQ6SLYbIom8ZFQ==
  hash W/eEUdBJo68M/+E2wvGpprk...

accountant2  Maple2026!
  salt yWxLOpmr1DkBA3zvgFiW4A==
  hash 3SEs1JxQpix/1qAPz8ftnsE...
    Sources: https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
    

    2.5 Pepper and work factor
    

    Slide 25Pepper and work factor (key stretching)
    • Pepper: one secret value added to all passwords, stored outside the database (configuration, HSM (Hardware Security Module))
    • Key stretching: a deliberately slow, tunable hash · Work factor: the tunable cost
    • One login pays about 0.2 s; an attacker pays it for every guess
    • Memory-hard: needs a large amount of RAM (Random-Access Memory) per guess, which limits GPU (Graphics Processing Unit) cracking
    FunctionRecommended setting (OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project))
    Argon2id (memory-hard)m = 19 MiB (mebibytes, 2^20 bytes each), t = 2, p = 1
    scrypt (memory-hard)N = 2¹⁷ (128 MiB (mebibytes, 2^20 bytes each)), r = 8, p = 1
    bcryptwork factor 10 or more; reads only 72 bytes
    PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 using HMAC with SHA-256)600,000 iterations
    yescrypt (memory-hard)default for /etc/shadow on Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora
    Sources: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html · https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106
    

    2.6 Where operating systems keep password hashes
    

    Slide 26Where systems keep password hashes (1/2)
    • Linux: names in /etc/passwd (readable by all) · hashes in /etc/shadow (root only)
    • Hash field: $id$salt$hash (yescrypt adds a parameter field)
    • Windows: SAM (Security Account Manager) (local accounts) and the Active Directory database store the unsalted NT (New Technology) hash: protect them
    

    Table 2.2 — Method identifiers in /etc/shadow (from crypt(5))
    PrefixMethodStatus in crypt(5)
    $y$yescryptRecommended for new hashes
    $gy$gost-yescryptRecommended for new hashes
    $7$scryptListed
    $2b$bcryptListed
    $6$sha512cryptAcceptable for new hashes
    $5$sha256cryptAcceptable for new hashes
    $1$md5cryptObsolete; do not use
    

    Sources: https://manpages.ubuntu.com/manpages/noble/man5/crypt.5.html
    

    Slide 27Where systems keep password hashes (2/2): reading a record
    • On your LAB_02 machine NM-LX01: sudo cat /etc/shadow and read the $y$ records. Reading the format is the exercise; cracking is not part of this course
    See Figure 2.2 in the Visualization part of this lesson: two real records, field by field.
    

    2.7 Verifying safely, and choosing good passwords
    

    Slide 28Verifying safely and choosing good passwords
    • Constant-time comparison: always compares every byte, so time reveals nothing (Python hmac.compare_digest)
    • NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) SP (Special Publication) 800-63B-4 (2025): at least 15 characters when the password is the only factor; at least 8 with MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication)
    • Accept at least 64 characters · no composition rules · no forced periodic changes (unless compromised)
    • Check new passwords against a blocklist of common and breached passwords
    • Pwned Passwords: only 5 characters of the SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1) hash leave your computer
    • MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) makes a stolen password insufficient; a password manager makes long, unique passwords practical
    15+characters for a single-factor password (NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology), 2025)
    Sources: https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/63/b/4/final · https://haveibeenpwned.com/Passwords · https://docs.python.org/3/library/hmac.html
    

    Key terms of Lesson 2
    Enrollment / verification
    Enrollment stores the hash of a new password; verification hashes the typed password with the same method and compares.
    Lookup table / rainbow table
    Precomputed tables that map hashes back to passwords; a rainbow table stores chains to save space. Both fail against salted hashes.
    Salt
    A unique random value per password, combined with it before hashing and stored in clear; defeats precomputed tables and hides password reuse.
    Pepper
    A secret value added to all passwords and stored outside the database.
    Key stretching / work factor
    Making each hash deliberately expensive (iterations, cost, memory) so that each guess costs the attacker time.
    Memory-hard function
    A password-hashing function that needs a large amount of RAM (Random-Access Memory) per guess (scrypt, Argon2id, yescrypt), which limits parallel cracking on GPUs (Graphics Processing Units).
    /etc/shadow
    The Linux file, readable only by root, that stores password hashes in the format $id$salt$hash.
    NT (New Technology) hash
    The Windows password hash: MD4 (Message Digest 4) of the password, not salted.
    Constant-time comparison
    A comparison that always takes the same time, so response time reveals nothing about the stored value.

    Real-life example 2 Choosing how NorthMaple stores staff passwords
    Slide 30Real-life example 2: how NorthMaple stores staff passwords
    

    The task of this example
    Before any NorthMaple service gets a login page, decide and prove how staff passwords will be stored: compare an unsalted SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) table with a salted PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) store, and show how a login is verified.
    How it relates to Lesson 2: The example applies sections 2.2 to 2.5: hash-based verification, the weaknesses of fast unsalted hashes, the effect of a salt, and the work factor.
    The situation
    NorthMaple's role table has three accountants, two technicians and a receptionist. Two accountants chose the same password, Maple2026!, and the receptionist chose Summer2026 (lab-only values). The IT (Information Technology) administrator stores the passwords twice: once the wrong way (plain SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output)), once the right way (PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 using HMAC with SHA-256), 16-byte random salt, 600,000 iterations). Then he plays the attacker with a small list of common passwords, and measures the cost of one guess in each case.
    Where it comes back in the course
    Today's guided exercise: you hash a password with openssl passwd -6, once with a random salt and once with a fixed salt, and observe the difference. LAB_02 (done): the users you created on NM-LX01 already have salted yescrypt hashes in /etc/shadow. LAB_06, part 1 (Class 16): WireGuard authenticates the remote worker with a key pair instead of a password. Final Project, Chapter 7: rows 2 (repeated password guessing against the remote access) and 9 (default credentials on network devices) need exactly this reasoning.
    Deliverable you will reuse
    A credential-storage decision table: method, salt length, work factor, where the records are stored, who can read them, and the measured cost of one guess. You will reuse it to justify rows 2 and 9 of the resilience assessment.
    

    Code 2 c14_L2_password_store.py
    

    ⚠ Lab only (Legal Notice, sections 3 and 4)
    Run Code 2 only inside your isolated laboratory, on your own lab machines, never against a system, account or communication that is not yours. The four passwords are lab-made. Never test real passwords, and never run it on hashes copied from a real system.
    

    

    What this code does and how it relates to the lecture
    The script stores four lab accounts in two ways and compares them. Part A uses plain SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output): it shows that two identical passwords produce identical digests and that a precomputed table recovers three of four passwords at once. Part B uses a salted PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 using HMAC with SHA-256) record with 600,000 iterations: the same table recovers nothing, a correct and a wrong login are verified with a constant-time comparison, and the cost of one guess is measured for both methods. It illustrates sections 2.2, 2.3, 2.4, 2.5 and 2.7.
    

    Run it in your lab: Any system with Python 3: python3 c14_L2_password_store.py. Salts are random, so the stored records change at every run; the unsalted SHA-256 values never change, which is exactly the problem.
    

    c14_L2_password_store.py · Python 3 (standard library only)






Step 0
    

    #!/usr/bin/env python3
# =============================================================================
# c14_L2_password_store.py         Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) - Class 14
# TASK: Decide how NorthMaple stores staff passwords before any company service
#       gets a login page. The script compares two storage methods:
#         (A) an unsalted, fast SHA-256 hash   -> the WRONG way
#         (B) a salted, slow PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hash (600,000 iterations) -> the RIGHT way
#       and shows how a login is verified against the stored record.
# LAB ONLY: fictional accounts and lab-only passwords. Never use real ones.
# Needs: Python 3 only (standard library).
# =============================================================================

# Load the standard hash library: it provides sha256() and pbkdf2_hmac().
import hashlib
# Load the HMAC module: we only use compare_digest(), a comparison that takes the same time whatever the input.
import hmac
# Load the operating-system module: os.urandom() gives cryptographically secure random bytes for the salts.
import os
# Load base64: it turns raw bytes (salt, hash) into printable text that can be stored in a file or database.
import base64
# Load the timeit module: it runs a small piece of code many times and measures the average duration precisely.
import timeit

# The four lab accounts of the NorthMaple role table; two accountants chose the SAME password on purpose.
staff = {"accountant1": "Maple2026!", "accountant2": "Maple2026!", "technician1": "orbit-candle-river-velvet-42", "reception": "Summer2026"}
# The number of PBKDF2 iterations (work factor); 600,000 is the value OWASP recommends for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256.
ITERATIONS = 600_000

# (A) STEP 1 - The wrong way: store the plain SHA-256 of each password, with no salt.
unsalted = {user: hashlib.sha256(pw.encode()).hexdigest() for user, pw in staff.items()}
# Print each stored value; we show the first 16 hexadecimal characters only, to keep the lines short.
for user, digest in unsalted.items():
    # One line per account: the same password always produces exactly the same digest.
    print(f"[A1] {user:<12} sha256 = {digest[:16]}...")

# (A) STEP 2 - Count how many accounts share each digest; a count above 1 reveals password reuse to anyone who reads the table.
reused = [user for user in unsalted if list(unsalted.values()).count(unsalted[user]) > 1]
# Print the accounts that leak the fact that they share a password.
print(f"[A2] Identical digests (shared password visible): {reused}")

# (A) STEP 3 - The attacker hashes a small list of common passwords ONCE, before seeing any victim (a precomputed table).
wordlist = ["123456", "password", "qwerty", "Welcome1", "Summer2026", "Maple2026!", "Montreal2026"]
# Build the lookup table "digest -> password"; because there is no salt, one table works against every system.
lookup = {hashlib.sha256(word.encode()).hexdigest(): word for word in wordlist}
# Look up every stolen digest in the table; a hit reveals the password instantly, with no further computation.
cracked = {user: lookup[digest] for user, digest in unsalted.items() if digest in lookup}
# Print the result of the lookup attack against the unsalted table.
print(f"[A3] Cracked by table lookup: {len(cracked)} of {len(unsalted)} -> {cracked}")

# (B) STEP 4 - The right way: a function that turns one password into one salted, slow, self-describing record.
def hash_password(password: str) -> str:
    # Draw a new random 16-byte (128-bit) salt for this password; it is unique per account and per change.
    salt = os.urandom(16)
    # Derive a 32-byte hash with PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256: salt + password, repeated ITERATIONS times on purpose.
    derived = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", password.encode(), salt, ITERATIONS)
    # Return one text record: algorithm $ iterations $ salt $ hash; the salt is stored in clear, it is not a secret.
    return f"pbkdf2_sha256${ITERATIONS}${base64.b64encode(salt).decode()}${base64.b64encode(derived).decode()}"

# (B) STEP 5 - Create the salted record for every account; this is what the company database would contain.
store = {user: hash_password(pw) for user, pw in staff.items()}
# Print each record shortened: algorithm, iterations, salt and the start of the hash.
for user, record in store.items():
    # Split the record on "$" to display its four fields separately.
    algo, iters, salt_b64, hash_b64 = record.split("$")
    # The two accountants now have different salts, so their stored hashes differ as well.
    print(f"[B5] {user:<12} {algo} {iters} salt={salt_b64} hash={hash_b64[:12]}...")

# (B) STEP 6 - Run the attacker's precomputed table against the salted records.
cracked_salted = [user for user, record in store.items() if record.split("$")[3] in lookup]
# Nothing matches: every salt would require a separate table, computed at the slow PBKDF2 speed.
print(f"[B6] Cracked by table lookup after salting: {len(cracked_salted)} of {len(store)}")

# (B) STEP 7 - The login check: a function that tests a typed password against a stored record.
def verify_password(typed: str, record: str) -> bool:
    # Read back the algorithm, the iteration count, the salt and the stored hash from the record.
    algo, iters, salt_b64, hash_b64 = record.split("$")
    # Recompute the hash of the typed password with the SAME salt and the SAME iteration count.
    candidate = hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", typed.encode(), base64.b64decode(salt_b64), int(iters))
    # Compare in constant time; an ordinary "==" can stop at the first different byte and leak timing information.
    return hmac.compare_digest(candidate, base64.b64decode(hash_b64))

# Verify the correct password of accountant1: the recomputed hash equals the stored hash.
print(f"[B7] Login accountant1 with 'Maple2026!'  -> {verify_password('Maple2026!', store['accountant1'])}")
# Verify a wrong password: a single different character gives a completely different hash.
print(f"[B7] Login accountant1 with 'maple2026!'  -> {verify_password('maple2026!', store['accountant1'])}")

# (B) STEP 8 - Measure the average cost of ONE fast SHA-256 hash, averaged over 100,000 runs (the attacker's cost per guess against table A).
fast = timeit.timeit(lambda: hashlib.sha256(b"Maple2026!").digest(), number=100_000) / 100_000
# Measure the cost of ONE PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 hash with 600,000 iterations (the attacker's cost per guess against store B).
slow = timeit.timeit(lambda: hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac("sha256", b"Maple2026!", os.urandom(16), ITERATIONS), number=1)
# Print both times and their ratio: every single guess costs the attacker this many times more work.
print(f"[B8] One SHA-256: {fast * 1e6:.2f} us | one PBKDF2 (600k): {slow * 1e3:.0f} ms | about {slow / fast:,.0f} times slower per guess")

      Live visualization
      

      Replay of a real run recorded on September 30, 2026 (Ubuntu, Python 3.11, cryptography 46.0.7, OpenSSL 3.0.13). Keys, salts and nonces are random, so your own run prints different values; the logic and the results are the same.
      Step-by-step explanation
      1. Imports. hashlib (SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) and PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2)), hmac (constant-time comparison), os (random salts), base64 (printable storage), timeit (measurements). All are part of Python's standard library.
      2. Accounts and work factor. The dictionary staff holds four lab accounts; two share a password on purpose. ITERATIONS = 600_000 is the OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) value for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2 using HMAC with SHA-256).
      3. Step 1 (A), unsalted storage. A dictionary comprehension stores sha256(password) for each user. The loop prints the first 16 hexadecimal characters: accountant1 and accountant2 show the same value.
      4. Step 2 (A), reuse detection. Counting identical digests lists the accounts that share a password. Anyone who reads the table learns this.
      5. Step 3 (A), precomputed table. The attacker hashes a wordlist once and builds a dictionary digest → password. Each stolen digest is looked up; three accounts fall with no further computation.
      6. Step 4 (B), hash_password(). For each password, a new 16-byte salt comes from os.urandom; pbkdf2_hmac repeats HMAC-SHA-256 (Hash-based Message Authentication Code with Secure Hash Algorithm 256) 600,000 times; the function returns one self-describing record algorithm$iterations$salt$hash.
      7. Step 5 (B), the salted store. The loop prints each record. The two accountants now have different salts and different hashes, although their passwords are identical.
      8. Step 6 (B), the table again. None of the stored hashes appears in the attacker's table: 0 of 4.
      9. Step 7 (B), verify_password(). The function splits the record, recomputes PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) with the stored salt and iteration count, and compares with hmac.compare_digest. The correct password returns True; a single wrong character (lower-case m) returns False.
      10. Step 8 (B), the cost of one guess. timeit averages 100,000 SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) computations, then times one PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2). The ratio, about 200,000 on the recording machine, is the factor by which every guess becomes more expensive for the attacker.

      Where cryptography protects data: in transit and at rest
      

      

      

      

      Slide 31Where cryptography protects data
      

      Data in transit and data at rest.
      

      3.1 The three states of data3.2 Protecting data in transit3.3 Protecting data at rest3.4 Key management3.5 Why the law caresVideosReal-life exampleCodeVisualizationFlashcardsQuestions
      

      3.1 The three states of data
      

      Slide 32The three states of data
      At rest
      Stored: disks, SSDs (Solid-State Drives), USB (Universal Serial Bus) drives, backups, databases, cloud storage
      In transit
      Moving on a network: LAN (Local Area Network), Wi-Fi, Internet, VPN (Virtual Private Network) tunnel
      In use
      Being processed in RAM (Random-Access Memory) by the CPU (Central Processing Unit): protected by operating-system access control
      • One file, three states: the ledger on NM-FS01 (at rest) → WireGuard to NM-RW01 (in transit) → opened in a spreadsheet (in use)
      • A control that protects one state does nothing for the others
      

      3.2 Protecting data in transit
      

      Slide 33Data in transit (1/2): TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3
      • Threats: eavesdropping (T1040), modification, impersonation
      • TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 (RFC (Request for Comments) 8446, 2018) in two phases:
        • Handshake: versions, cipher suites, ephemeral ECDHE (Elliptic-Curve Diffie–Hellman Ephemeral) key shares, certificate, signature → session keys
        • Record protocol: data encrypted with AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data)
      • Forward secrecy: a stolen server key cannot decrypt recorded past sessions
      • HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) = HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) inside TLS (TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) 443) · TLS 1.0 and 1.1 deprecated (RFC (Request for Comments) 8996)
      


      Sources: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8446 · https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996
      

      Slide 34Data in transit (2/2): other protocols and proof
      • SSH (Secure Shell) (port 22): administration, SFTP/SCP (SFTP: SSH File Transfer Protocol; SCP: Secure Copy Protocol) · IPsec (Internet Protocol Security) (ESP (Encapsulating Security Payload), IKE (Internet Key Exchange)): site-to-site VPNs (Virtual Private Networks)
      • WireGuard: Curve25519 keys, ChaCha20-Poly1305, counter-based replay protection (LAB_06)
      • WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3): protects the radio link only
      • Link encryption (hop by hop) vs end-to-end encryption (sender to final receiver)
      • WireGuard NM-RW01 → NM-FW01: tunnel encryption across café Wi-Fi and the Internet
      • Prove it: Wireshark shows only TLS (Transport Layer Security) Application Data; openssl s_client shows the version
      Recorded run of Code 3, Part C
      $ openssl s_client -connect 127.0.0.1:8443 \
    -tls1_3 -brief
Protocol version: TLSv1.3
Ciphersuite: TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384

$ ... -tls1_2 ...
[C2] TLS 1.2 REFUSED
      Sources: https://www.wireguard.com/protocol/ · https://www.wireshark.org/
      

      3.3 Protecting data at rest
      

      Slide 35Data at rest (1/2): full-disk encryption
      • Threats: lost or stolen laptop (resilience row 5), discarded disks, stolen backups, open cloud buckets
      • Full-disk encryption: the whole volume; transparent after unlock
      • BitLocker: XTS-AES (Advanced Encryption Standard in XEX-based Tweaked-codebook mode with ciphertext Stealing) 128 by default, TPM (Trusted Platform Module) checks boot integrity · LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup) (cryptsetup) · FileVault
      • Limit: protects a device that is off, hibernated or at the pre-boot unlock screen
      • It does not protect a running system, even screen-locked, nor stop ransomware running as the user
      OFF
      Disk = ciphertext without the key
      RUNNING
      The OS (Operating System) decrypts for every process, malware included
      Sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/security/operating-system-security/data-protection/bitlocker/
      

      Slide 36Data at rest (2/2): files, databases and cloud
      • File and container encryption: EFS (Encrypting File System), VeraCrypt, 7-Zip AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key), GnuPG, openssl enc
        • Containers and encrypted archives keep their protection when copied; EFS (Encrypting File System) only while on NTFS (New Technology File System)
        • openssl enc gives confidentiality only: it does not support GCM (Galois/Counter Mode)
      • Databases: TDE (Transparent Data Encryption) encrypts the database files; column-level encryption for specific fields
      • Cloud: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) encrypts every new object since January 5, 2023 (SSE-S3 (Server-Side Encryption with Amazon S3 managed keys), AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key))
        • Azure Storage encryption is always on (AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key)), Microsoft- or customer-managed keys
      • Shared responsibility: provider encryption does not protect a bucket you made public
      Sources: https://veracrypt.io/ · https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-enc/ · https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/default-encryption-faq.html · https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/storage/common/storage-service-encryption
      

      3.4 Key management
      

      Slide 37Key management
      • Once data is encrypted, its security depends on the protection of the keys
      • Generate keys with a CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator), never from a guessable value
      • Store keys apart from the data: TPM (Trusted Platform Module), HSM (Hardware Security Module), cloud KMS (Key Management Service), file mode 600
      • Back up recovery keys (BitLocker: a 48-digit number)
      • Rotate and revoke: remove a lost device's WireGuard peer at once
      • Destroy every copy of a key = crypto-erase
      Generate→Store→Back up→Rotate / revoke→Destroy
      

      3.5 Why the law cares
      

      Slide 38Why the law cares
      • NorthMaple holds client financial records: personal information
      • PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act), Schedule 1, 4.7.1: safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
      • 4.7.3 (c): "technological measures, for example, the use of passwords and encryption"
      • Québec Law 25: notify the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec) and the persons concerned promptly when a confidentiality incident presents a risk of serious injury; keep an incident register
      • A lost laptop that is fully encrypted, key not exposed: misuse is much less likely
      • Educational context, not legal advice (Legal Notice, section 7)
      Sources: https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/P-8.6/FullText.html · https://www.cai.gouv.qc.ca/protection-renseignements-personnels/information-entreprises-privees/incidents-confidentialite-mesures-securite-entreprises
      

      Key terms of Lesson 3
      Data at rest / in transit / in use
      Stored data; data moving across a network; data being processed in memory by the CPU (Central Processing Unit).
      Eavesdropping
      Passive capture of network traffic to read its content (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1040).
      TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshake
      The first phase of TLS (Transport Layer Security): version and cipher-suite negotiation, ephemeral key exchange, server authentication by certificate, derivation of session keys.
      Forward secrecy
      Session keys come from ephemeral key exchanges, so a later theft of the server's long-term private key does not decrypt recorded sessions.
      Link vs end-to-end encryption
      Link encryption protects one segment and is removed at each device; end-to-end encryption protects data from sender to final receiver.
      Full-disk encryption
      Encryption of a whole volume (BitLocker, LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup), FileVault); protects a powered-off or hibernated device, not a running system, even with the screen locked.
      File or container encryption
      Encryption of selected files or an encrypted container (EFS (Encrypting File System), VeraCrypt, 7-Zip AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key), GnuPG); for containers and encrypted archives the protection travels with the copied file.
      Key management
      Generation, storage, backup, rotation, revocation and destruction of keys; the key must be stored apart from the data.
      Crypto-erase
      Making encrypted data permanently unreadable by destroying every copy of its key.

      Real-life example 3 Proving that the client-records folder is protected at rest and in transit
      Slide 40Real-life example 3: proving protection at rest and in transit
      

      The task of this example
      Produce three pieces of evidence for NorthMaple's owner and for the Final Project grader: (A) the encrypted client-records archive cannot be read without its key; (B) the copy received by the remote worker is bit-for-bit identical to the original; (C) the service that delivers files accepts TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 only.
      How it relates to Lesson 3: Part A is data at rest (section 3.3), Parts B and C are data in transit (section 3.2), and the separate, protected key file applies key management (section 3.4).
      The situation
      The owner of NorthMaple asks a simple question after reading about a stolen laptop in the news: "Can you show me that our client files are protected?" Saying "yes, we encrypt" is not evidence. The IT (Information Technology) administrator runs one script on the Linux workstation NM-LX01 and pastes its output into the evidence folder: the archive before and after encryption, a failed attempt with a wrong key, two identical SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digests, and a TLS (Transport Layer Security) test that shows version 1.3 accepted and version 1.2 refused.
      Where it comes back in the course
      LAB_06, part 2 (Class 17): you encrypt one folder or volume of company data, enable HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) on one internal service, and validate both; the grading requires that the encrypted data be proven inaccessible without its key and that the service answer only over HTTPS. Today's guided exercise: you hash a file and verify its integrity, which is Part B. Final Project, Chapter 7: rows 5 (lost or stolen laptop) and 6 (remote worker's traffic intercepted on public Wi-Fi).
      Deliverable you will reuse
      An encryption validation sheet with three sections (at rest, integrity in transit, TLS (Transport Layer Security) version), each with the command, the expected result and the observed result. This is the structure of section N.4 (Validation) of the chapter template in your Course Procedure Manual.
      

      Code 3 c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh
      

      ⚠ Lab only (Legal Notice, sections 3 and 4)
      Run Code 3 only inside your isolated laboratory, on your own lab machines, never against a system, account or communication that is not yours. The TLS (Transport Layer Security) test server listens on your own machine only; do not point the TLS checks at servers you do not own.
      

      

      What this code does and how it relates to the lecture
      The script builds a small fictional client-records folder, archives it, encrypts the archive with AES-256 (key derived with PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2), 600,000 iterations), and shows that the encrypted file cannot be listed or decrypted with a wrong key (Part A, at rest). It then compares SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) digests before and after a simulated transfer (Part B, integrity in transit) and tests a TLS (Transport Layer Security) server with OpenSSL to show that TLS 1.3 is accepted and TLS 1.2 is refused (Part C). It illustrates sections 3.2, 3.3 and 3.4.
      

      Run it in your lab: On NM-LX01 or NM-RW01: bash c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh (uses a local test server) or bash c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh 192.168.20.10:443 to test your own internal service in LAB_06. Everything happens in a temporary folder that is deleted at the end.
      

      c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh · Bash + OpenSSL (Ubuntu)






Step 0
      

      #!/usr/bin/env bash
# =============================================================================
# c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh  Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) - Class 14
# TASK: Produce the evidence that NorthMaple's client-records folder is protected
#         Part A - AT REST:     the encrypted archive cannot be read without its key;
#         Part B - IN TRANSIT:  the copy received by the remote worker is bit-for-bit
#                               identical to the original (SHA-256 comparison);
#         Part C - IN TRANSIT:  the service that delivers files accepts TLS 1.3 only.
# LAB ONLY: fictional data; run on NM-LX01 or NM-RW01 (Ubuntu) inside your lab.
# Usage:  bash c14_L3_rest_transit_evidence.sh [host:port]
#         Without an argument, Part C starts a throw-away local TLS test server.
# Needs:  bash, openssl, tar, sha256sum, od (all present on Ubuntu Server).
# =============================================================================

# Stop at the first failing command (-e), treat unset variables as errors (-u), and fail a pipeline if any part fails (-o pipefail).
set -euo pipefail
# Create a private working folder in /tmp with a random name, so the test never touches real data.
WORK="$(mktemp -d)"
# Move into that folder; every file of the exercise is created here.
cd "$WORK"
# Register a clean-up action that runs when the script ends: stop the test server (if any) and delete the folder.
trap 'kill "${SERVER_PID:-0}" 2>/dev/null || true; rm -rf "$WORK"' EXIT

# ---------------- PART A - DATA AT REST ----------------
# Create the folder that stands for NorthMaple's client records.
mkdir client-records
# Write a fictional ledger file (CSV = comma-separated values) into the folder.
printf 'client_id,client_name,balance_cad\nC-1001,Tremblay Renovations,48250.00\n' > client-records/ledger_Q3.csv
# Write a second fictional document, so the folder contains more than one file.
printf 'Engagement letter - Gagnon Dental Clinic - fiscal year 2026\n' > client-records/engagement_C-1002.txt
# Pack the folder into one compressed archive (tar + gzip) that can be encrypted as a single file.
tar -czf records.tgz client-records
# Show that, before encryption, anyone who obtains the archive can list its files and read a client name in it.
echo "[A1] Before encryption: files = $(tar -tzf records.tgz | tr '\n' ' ')| 'Tremblay' found $(tar -xzOf records.tgz | grep -c 'Tremblay') time(s)"
# Generate 32 random bytes (256 bits) encoded in Base64 and store them as the passphrase file (the key material).
openssl rand -base64 32 > records.key
# Restrict the key file to its owner only (read/write for the owner, nothing for others).
chmod 600 records.key
# Encrypt the archive: AES-256-CBC, key derived from the passphrase with PBKDF2 (600,000 iterations) and a random salt.
openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -salt -in records.tgz -out records.tgz.enc -pass file:records.key
# Delete the unencrypted archive, as a real procedure would do once encryption is confirmed.
rm records.tgz
# Display the first 32 bytes in hexadecimal with od (-A x: hex offsets, -t x1z: hex bytes + printable text): "Salted__" header, 8-byte salt, ciphertext.
echo "[A2] First 32 bytes of records.tgz.enc:" && od -A x -t x1z -N 32 records.tgz.enc
# Try to list the encrypted file as if it were an archive; tar fails because the bytes are now ciphertext.
if tar -tzf records.tgz.enc >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    # This branch would mean the encrypted file can still be opened as an archive; it must not happen.
    echo "[A3] WARNING: the encrypted file can be listed"
# Otherwise tar could not recognize any archive structure.
else
    # Record the evidence: file names and contents are no longer visible to someone who copies the file.
    echo "[A3] Encrypted file cannot be listed or read: names and contents are hidden"
# End of the if/else test.
fi
# Create a second, wrong passphrase file to simulate someone who has the file but not the key.
openssl rand -base64 32 > wrong.key
# Try to decrypt with the wrong key; errors are hidden and ignored because failure is the expected result.
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in records.tgz.enc -out wrong.out -pass file:wrong.key 2>/dev/null || true
# Check whether the output of the wrong-key attempt is a readable archive; tar fails because the bytes are meaningless.
if tar -tzf wrong.out >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    # This branch would mean the data is readable without the key; it must not happen.
    echo "[A4] WARNING: data readable with a wrong key"
# Otherwise the attempt produced no usable data.
else
    # Record the expected evidence: without the correct key, the stored data stays unreadable.
    echo "[A4] Wrong key -> no readable archive: data at rest is protected"
# End of the if/else test.
fi

# ---------------- PART B - DATA IN TRANSIT: INTEGRITY ----------------
# Decrypt with the correct key to get the original archive back (the sender's reference copy).
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in records.tgz.enc -out records.tgz -pass file:records.key
# Compute the SHA-256 digest of the original archive and keep only the 64-character value (first field).
SENT="$(sha256sum records.tgz | cut -d' ' -f1)"
# Print the digest recorded before the transfer.
echo "[B1] SHA-256 before transfer: $SENT"
# Simulate the transfer: in LAB_06 this copy travels through the VPN (for example with scp); here it is a local copy.
cp records.tgz.enc received.tgz.enc
# The remote worker decrypts the received file with the key, which was delivered separately and securely.
openssl enc -d -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -in received.tgz.enc -out received.tgz -pass file:records.key
# Compute the SHA-256 digest of the received archive.
RECEIVED="$(sha256sum received.tgz | cut -d' ' -f1)"
# Print the digest measured after the transfer.
echo "[B2] SHA-256 after transfer:  $RECEIVED"
# Compare both digests as text; equal strings mean identical files.
if [ "$SENT" = "$RECEIVED" ]; then
    # Record the evidence of integrity.
    echo "[B3] MATCH - the received copy is bit-for-bit identical"
# Different digests mean the file changed (corruption or tampering).
else
    # Record the failure; the file must not be used.
    echo "[B3] MISMATCH - do not use the received file"
# End of the comparison.
fi

# ---------------- PART C - DATA IN TRANSIT: TLS VERSION ----------------
# Use the host:port given as the first argument, or the local test address when no argument is given.
TARGET="${1:-127.0.0.1:8443}"
# When no argument was given, prepare a throw-away local server for the demonstration.
if [ -z "${1:-}" ]; then
    # Create a one-day self-signed certificate and its private key (certificates are the topic of Class 15).
    openssl req -x509 -newkey rsa:2048 -nodes -keyout demo.key -out demo.crt -days 1 -subj "/CN=nm-demo.lab" 2>/dev/null
    # Start a test TLS server that accepts TLS 1.3 only, in the background (&).
    openssl s_server -accept 8443 -cert demo.crt -key demo.key -tls1_3 -www -quiet >/dev/null 2>&1 &
    # Remember the process number of the server so the clean-up action can stop it.
    SERVER_PID=$!
    # Wait one second so the server is ready before the client connects.
    sleep 1
# End of the test-server preparation.
fi
# Connect with TLS 1.3 and keep only the lines that report the negotiated protocol version and cipher suite.
echo "[C1] TLS 1.3 connection to $TARGET:" && echo | openssl s_client -connect "$TARGET" -tls1_3 -brief 2>&1 | grep -E "Protocol version|Ciphersuite"
# Try the older TLS 1.2; a server configured for TLS 1.3 only must refuse the handshake.
if echo | openssl s_client -connect "$TARGET" -tls1_2 -brief >/dev/null 2>&1; then
    # This branch means the older protocol is still accepted: a finding to correct.
    echo "[C2] TLS 1.2 ACCEPTED - older protocol still enabled"
# The handshake failed, which is the expected result.
else
    # Record the evidence that the old protocol version is refused.
    echo "[C2] TLS 1.2 REFUSED - server accepts TLS 1.3 only"
# End of the protocol test.
fi

        Replay of a real run recorded on September 30, 2026 (Ubuntu, Python 3.11, cryptography 46.0.7, OpenSSL 3.0.13). Keys, salts and nonces are random, so your own run prints different values; the logic and the results are the same.
        Step-by-step explanation
        1. Safety settings. set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first error. mktemp -d creates a private working folder; trap ... EXIT guarantees that the test server is stopped and the folder deleted, even after an error.
        2. Part A, preparation. mkdir and two printf commands create the fictional folder; tar -czf packs it into one archive. Line [A1] proves that, before encryption, anyone can list the files and find a client name.
        3. Part A, the key. openssl rand -base64 32 draws 256 random bits for the passphrase file; chmod 600 makes it readable by its owner only (key management).
        4. Part A, encryption. openssl enc -aes-256-cbc -pbkdf2 -iter 600000 -salt derives the AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key from the passphrase with PBKDF2 (Password-Based Key Derivation Function 2) and a random salt, then encrypts. The clear archive is deleted.
        5. Part A, evidence. od shows the first 32 bytes: the text Salted__, 8 salt bytes, then ciphertext [A2]. tar -tzf cannot list the encrypted file [A3]. A decryption attempt with a second random key produces no readable archive [A4].
        6. Part B, integrity. The archive is decrypted with the right key and its SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) is stored in SENT [B1]. The encrypted file is copied (in LAB_06 it travels through the VPN (Virtual Private Network)), decrypted on the receiving side, and hashed into RECEIVED [B2]. The string comparison prints MATCH [B3].
        7. Part C, the test server. Without an argument, the script creates a one-day self-signed certificate and starts openssl s_server -tls1_3 in the background, a server that accepts TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.3 only.
        8. Part C, the checks. openssl s_client -tls1_3 -brief prints the negotiated version and cipher suite [C1]: TLSv1.3 and TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384. A second connection forced to -tls1_2 fails, and the script records that the old version is refused [C2].

        Slide 42Attacks on cryptosystems and simple defenses
        

        Awareness level.
        

        4.1 Attacks on keys and passwords4.2 Attacks on the communication4.3 Attacks on algorithms, and the quantum…4.4 Attacks on the implementation4.5 Attacks on key management and on peopl…VideosReal-life exampleCodeVisualizationFlashcardsQuestions
        

        4.1 Attacks on keys and passwords
        

        Slide 43Attacks on keys and passwords (1/2): exhaustive search
        • Cryptanalysis: the study of methods for defeating cryptographic protection
        • Brute-force attack: try every key; average time = (alphabet^length ÷ 2) ÷ guesses per second
        • Random AES-128 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit key) key at 10¹² keys/s: about 5.4 × 10¹⁸ years (the universe: 1.4 × 10¹⁰ years)
        • Exhaustive search works only against short or human-chosen passwords
        • Dictionary attack: words from leaked-password lists (rockyou.txt)
        • Rule-based attack: predictable changes: Summer2026, Maple2026!
        5.4 × 10¹⁸years to exhaust half of the AES-128 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit key) key space at 10¹² keys/s
        

        Slide 44Attacks on keys and passwords (2/2): online vs offline
        • Precomputed tables (defeated by salts) · Password spraying · Credential stuffing (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1110)
        • Online attack: through the live login → rate limiting, lockout, MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication), IDS (Intrusion Detection System) alerts · Offline attack: stolen hashes → only password strength and work factor
        See Figure 4.2 in the Visualization part of this lesson: online and offline password attacks.
        Sources: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1110/
        

        4.2 Attacks on the communication
        

        Slide 45Attacks on the communication
        • On-path attack (man-in-the-middle): ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning, DHCP (Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol) spoofing, evil twin (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1557)
          • Defense: authenticated key exchange: validate certificates, never accept a certificate warning, VPN (Virtual Private Network), WPA3 (Wi-Fi Protected Access 3)
          • HSTS (HTTP Strict Transport Security) (RFC (Request for Comments) 6797) forces HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) and blocks SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) stripping after the first visit, or from the first visit for preloaded sites
        • Downgrade attack: force an old version or weak cipher; POODLE (Padding Oracle On Downgraded Legacy Encryption) on SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) 3.0 (CVE-2014-3566 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures))
          • Defense: disable SSL (Secure Sockets Layer), TLS (Transport Layer Security) 1.0 and TLS 1.1; TLS 1.3 has a built-in downgrade signal
        • Replay attack: resend a captured valid message
          • Defense: nonces, timestamps, counters (WireGuard rejects old counters)
        Sources: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1557/ · https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6797 · https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-3566
        

        4.3 Attacks on algorithms, and the quantum question
        

        Slide 46Attacks on algorithms, and the quantum question
        • Collision attack / birthday attack: two inputs, same hash; about 2^(n/2) attempts
        • MD5 (Message Digest 5): the Flame malware carried a forged code-signing certificate (2012) · SHA-1 (Secure Hash Algorithm 1): SHAttered (2017) → use SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) or SHA-3 (Secure Hash Algorithm 3)
        • Quantum: Shor's algorithm would break RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman) and ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography); Grover only halves AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) strength (AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key) stays strong)
        • Harvest now, decrypt later → post-quantum cryptography: FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 203 (ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism)), 204 (ML-DSA (Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm)), 205 (SLH-DSA (Stateless Hash-Based Digital Signature Algorithm))
        • Crypto-agility: replace algorithms without rebuilding systems
        Aug 2024
        NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology) publishes FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 203, 204, 205
        Apr 2026
        Canada: departmental migration plans
        End 2031
        High-priority systems migrated
        End 2035
        All systems migrated
        Sources: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/08/nist-releases-first-3-finalized-post-quantum-encryption-standards · https://www.cyber.gc.ca/en/guidance/roadmap-migration-post-quantum-cryptography-government-canada-itsm40001 · https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/security-updates/securityadvisories/2012/2718704
        

        4.4 Attacks on the implementation
        

        Slide 47Attacks on the implementation
        • Side-channel attack: time, power, emissions, cache → constant-time code · Mode misuse: ECB (Electronic Codebook) patterns, GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) nonce reuse · Weak random numbers → OS (Operating System) CSPRNG (Cryptographically Secure Pseudo-Random Number Generator)
        • Library flaws: Heartbleed (CVE-2014-0160 (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures)) → patching · Hard-coded keys → secrets manager · Never design your own crypto (OWASP (Open Worldwide Application Security Project) A04:2025)
        


        Sources: https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2014-0160 · https://top10.owasp.org/2025/A04_2025-Cryptographic_Failures/
        

        4.5 Attacks on key management and on people
        

        Slide 48Key theft, people, and ransomware
        • The easiest way to decrypt is to obtain the key: a copied private key, a recovery key in a shared folder, VPN (Virtual Private Network) credentials typed on a phishing page
        • Ransomware: attackers encrypt your data and demand payment (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1486); your own encryption does not prevent it
        Protect keys
        File mode 600, TPM (Trusted Platform Module) or HSM (Hardware Security Module)
        MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) and revocation
        Revoke lost devices at once
        Offline backups
        Immutable or offline copy (row 10)
        Layers
        Least privilege (LAB_02), detection (LAB_04), segmentation (LAB_05)
        Sources: https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1486/

        Key terms of Lesson 4
        Cryptanalysis
        The study of methods for defeating cryptographic protection.
        Brute-force attack
        Trying every possible key or password; average time = half the key space divided by the guess rate.
        Dictionary / rule-based attack
        Trying words from lists of real passwords, with the predictable modifications people apply.
        Password spraying / credential stuffing
        One common password against many accounts; stolen username-password pairs replayed on other services.
        Online vs offline attack
        Guessing against a live login (rate-limited, logged) versus guessing against stolen hashes on the attacker's own hardware.
        On-path (man-in-the-middle) attack
        An attacker relays and can read or alter traffic between two parties; defeated by authenticated key exchange and certificate validation.
        Downgrade attack
        Forcing the negotiation of an older protocol or weaker cipher; defeated by disabling old versions.
        Replay attack
        Resending a captured valid message; defeated by nonces, timestamps and counters.
        Collision / birthday attack
        Finding two inputs with the same hash; generic cost about 2^(n/2) for an n-bit hash.
        Side-channel attack
        Extracting secrets from time, power, emissions or cache behaviour of a computation; defeated by constant-time implementations.
        Harvest now, decrypt later / post-quantum cryptography
        Recording traffic today to decrypt it with a future quantum computer; answered by new algorithms such as ML-KEM (FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 203).
        Crypto-agility
        The ability to replace cryptographic algorithms without rebuilding systems.
