        Real-life example 4 Rating NorthMaple's passwords and keys against exhaustive search
        Slide 51Real-life example 4: rating NorthMaple's secrets
        

        The task of this example
        For each kind of secret NorthMaple uses (short passwords, long passwords, a passphrase, AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) keys) and each attack situation (online guessing, stolen fast hash, stolen slow hash, dedicated hardware), compute the average exhaustive-search time and give the verdict the resilience checklist asks for: Withstands, Partly or Does not.
        How it relates to Lesson 4: The example applies the brute-force formula of section 4.1, the online versus offline distinction, and the effect of a work factor from Lesson 2.
        The situation
        The Final Project resilience assessment (Chapter 7) asks for one plain sentence per attack scenario. For row 2, "Repeated password guessing against the remote access", a student cannot simply write "our passwords are strong". With this page, the administrator shows that an 8-letter lower-case password survives online guessing through a rate-limited VPN (Virtual Private Network) login only because of the rate limit, falls in 10 seconds once an unsalted hash is stolen, and holds about 4 months behind a slow salted hash; and that a random AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) key is out of reach in every case. The course thresholds are: at least 100 years = Withstands, at least 30 days = Partly, less = Does not.
        Where it comes back in the course
        Final Project, Chapter 7: rows 2, 6 and 9. LAB_06, part 1 (Class 16): WireGuard replaces the remote worker's password with a random 256-bit key pair, which moves row 2 into the "key" rows of the table. LAB_04 (done): an IDS (Intrusion Detection System) rule that alerts on repeated failed logins is the monitoring part of the defense.
        Deliverable you will reuse
        A brute-force resilience table (secret, key space, scenario, average time, verdict) that you paste into Chapter 7 as the justification for row 2, with the assumptions stated underneath.
        

        Code 4 c14_L4_bruteforce_estimator.html
        

        ⚠ Lab only (Legal Notice, sections 3 and 4)
        Run Code 4 only inside your isolated laboratory, on your own lab machines, never against a system, account or communication that is not yours. The page only does arithmetic on the lengths and rates it contains and contacts no system. Never type a real password into any page or tool.
        

        

        What this code does and how it relates to the lecture
        The page lists nine cases (secret type + attack scenario with an assumed guess rate). For each case the script computes the key space (alphabet size to the power of the length), the average exhaustive-search time (half the key space divided by the rate), converts it into a readable unit, and assigns the verdict Withstands, Partly or Does not. It fills a table with a bar proportional to log10(seconds). It illustrates section 4.1 and feeds row 2 of the resilience assessment.
        

        Run it in your lab: Save the file and open it in any browser (double-click). It works offline. To test your own policy, edit one line of the ROWS list (alphabet, length, scenario) and reload the page. Use the button Open the real page below the runner to see it rendered.
        

        c14_L4_bruteforce_estimator.html · Self-contained HTML + JavaScript






Step 0
        

        <!DOCTYPE html>
<!-- ==========================================================================
c14_L4_bruteforce_estimator.html   Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) - Class 14
TASK: Rate NorthMaple's secrets (passwords, passphrases, encryption keys) against
      exhaustive (brute-force) search, to justify rows 2 and 6 of the Final
      Project resilience assessment. For every secret and attack scenario the
      page computes the key space, the AVERAGE time an exhaustive search needs,
      and a verdict in the checklist's own words: Withstands / Partly / Does not.
ASSUMED ATTACK RATES (orders of magnitude for teaching, not measurements):
      online guessing 10/s | stolen fast unsalted hash 10^10/s |
      stolen slow salted hash 10^4/s | dedicated key-search hardware 10^12/s
Open the file in any browser. It needs no Internet connection.
=========================================================================== -->
<!-- Open the HTML document and declare English as the language of its content. -->
<html lang="en">
<!-- The head holds information about the page; nothing in it is displayed as content. -->
<head>
<!-- Declare the UTF-8 character encoding so that every character is displayed correctly. -->
<meta charset="utf-8">
<!-- The text shown on the browser tab. -->
<title>NorthMaple - brute-force time estimator</title>
<!-- Open the style sheet (CSS rules) that controls how the page looks. -->
<style>
/* Page font, outer margin, course background colour and text colour. */
body { font-family: Calibri, Carlito, Arial, sans-serif; margin: 24px; background: #FAF7F2; color: #1f2328; }
/* The table uses single borders and the full page width. */
table { border-collapse: collapse; width: 100%; }
/* Every cell gets a thin border, inner spacing and left-aligned text. */
th, td { border: 1px solid #d6cfc4; padding: 6px 8px; text-align: left; font-size: 14px; }
/* The horizontal bar that shows log10(seconds): a longer bar means a longer search. */
.bar { height: 10px; background: #0E7C7B; border-radius: 3px; margin-bottom: 3px; }
/* Colours of the three verdicts: green, amber, rust. */
.Withstands { color: #1b7f3b; font-weight: bold; } .Partly { color: #9a6700; font-weight: bold; } .Does-not { color: #B5440C; font-weight: bold; }
/* The next tag closes the style sheet. */
</style>
<!-- Close the head. -->
</head>
<!-- The body holds everything that appears on the screen. -->
<body>
<!-- Main heading of the page. -->
<h1>NorthMaple: how long would an exhaustive search take?</h1>
<!-- The results table: the header row is written here, the data rows are added by the script below. -->
<table id="results"><thead><tr><th>Secret</th><th>Key space</th><th>Attack scenario (assumed rate)</th><th>Average time</th><th>log10(seconds)</th><th>Verdict</th></tr></thead><tbody></tbody></table>
<!-- A reminder printed under the table: the figures are valid for RANDOM secrets only. -->
<p>Figures assume secrets chosen at random. Human-chosen passwords fall to dictionary attacks far sooner.</p>
<!-- Open the program (JavaScript) that computes and displays the results. -->
<script>
// Assumed attack speeds, in guesses per second (see the header of this file).
const RATE = { online: 10, fastHash: 1e10, slowHash: 1e4, keySearch: 1e12 };
// Number of seconds in one year of 365.25 days; used to convert seconds into years.
const YEAR = 365.25 * 24 * 3600;
// The list of cases to evaluate: description, alphabet size, length in symbols, scenario and its rate.
const ROWS = [
  // Receptionist-style password (8 lowercase letters) guessed ONLINE through the VPN login, which is rate-limited.
  { secret: "8 lowercase letters", alphabet: 26, length: 8, scenario: "online guessing, rate-limited", rate: RATE.online },
  // The same password after its UNSALTED FAST hash was stolen: the attacker guesses offline at full GPU speed.
  { secret: "8 lowercase letters", alphabet: 26, length: 8, scenario: "offline, fast unsalted hash", rate: RATE.fastHash },
  // The same password stored as a SALTED SLOW hash (PBKDF2 600,000 iterations): every guess is expensive.
  { secret: "8 lowercase letters", alphabet: 26, length: 8, scenario: "offline, slow salted hash", rate: RATE.slowHash },
  // 8 characters drawn from all 95 printable keyboard characters, fast unsalted hash stolen.
  { secret: "8 printable characters", alphabet: 95, length: 8, scenario: "offline, fast unsalted hash", rate: RATE.fastHash },
  // 15 lowercase letters: the minimum length NIST SP 800-63B-4 requires for a single-factor password.
  { secret: "15 lowercase letters", alphabet: 26, length: 15, scenario: "offline, fast unsalted hash", rate: RATE.fastHash },
  // Passphrase of 4 words picked at random from a 7,776-word list, fast unsalted hash stolen.
  { secret: "4 random words (7,776-word list)", alphabet: 7776, length: 4, scenario: "offline, fast unsalted hash", rate: RATE.fastHash },
  // The same 4-word passphrase stored as a salted slow hash.
  { secret: "4 random words (7,776-word list)", alphabet: 7776, length: 4, scenario: "offline, slow salted hash", rate: RATE.slowHash },
  // A random 128-bit AES key: 2 possible values per bit, 128 bits, dedicated key-search hardware.
  { secret: "AES-128 key (random)", alphabet: 2, length: 128, scenario: "dedicated key-search hardware", rate: RATE.keySearch },
  // A random 256-bit key (AES-256, as used for data at rest), same hardware.
  { secret: "AES-256 key (random)", alphabet: 2, length: 256, scenario: "dedicated key-search hardware", rate: RATE.keySearch }
// Close the list of cases.
];
// Key space = alphabet ^ length: the number of different secrets that exist with these rules.
function keySpace(row) { return Math.pow(row.alphabet, row.length); }
// Average search time: on average the right secret is found after half of the key space has been tried.
function averageSeconds(row) { return keySpace(row) / 2 / row.rate; }
// Write a large number in scientific notation, for example 2.09 x 10^11.
function sci(x) { const [m, e] = x.toExponential(2).split("e"); return `${m} &times; 10<sup>${Number(e)}</sup>`; }
// Convert a duration in seconds into the most readable unit.
function readable(s) {
  // Under one minute: seconds.
  if (s < 60) return `${s.toFixed(1)} seconds`;
  // Under one hour: minutes.
  if (s < 3600) return `${(s / 60).toFixed(1)} minutes`;
  // Under one day: hours.
  if (s < 86400) return `${(s / 3600).toFixed(1)} hours`;
  // Under one year: days.
  if (s < YEAR) return `${(s / 86400).toFixed(1)} days`;
  // Under one million years: whole years with thousands separators.
  if (s < 1e6 * YEAR) return `${Math.round(s / YEAR).toLocaleString("en-CA")} years`;
  // Beyond that: years in scientific notation.
  return `${sci(s / YEAR)} years`;
// Close the readable() function.
}
// Verdict with the course thresholds: at least 100 years = Withstands, at least 30 days = Partly, less = Does not.
function verdict(s) { return s >= 100 * YEAR ? "Withstands" : s >= 30 * 86400 ? "Partly" : "Does not"; }
// Find the body of the results table, where the new rows will be inserted.
const tbody = document.querySelector("#results tbody");
// Evaluate every case of the list, one after the other.
for (const row of ROWS) {
  // Number of possible secrets for this case.
  const space = keySpace(row);
  // Average time the exhaustive search needs at the assumed rate.
  const seconds = averageSeconds(row);
  // Verdict for the resilience checklist.
  const v = verdict(seconds);
  // Create an empty table row.
  const tr = document.createElement("tr");
  // Fill the six cells; the bar width is log10(seconds) on a scale where 70 = 100 % of the cell.
  tr.innerHTML = `<td>${row.secret}</td><td>${sci(space)}</td><td>${row.scenario} (${row.rate.toLocaleString("en-CA")}/s)</td><td>${readable(seconds)}</td><td><div class="bar" style="width:${Math.max(2, Math.log10(seconds) / 70 * 100).toFixed(1)}%"></div>${Math.log10(seconds).toFixed(1)}</td><td class="${v.replace(" ", "-")}">${v}</td>`;
  // Add the finished row to the table, which makes it visible.
  tbody.appendChild(tr);
// Close the loop.
}
// The next tag closes the program.
</script>
<!-- Close the body. -->
</body>
<!-- Close the HTML document. -->
</html>

          Live visualization
          

          The steps are computed with the same formulas as the page; press Open the real page to see the browser render it.
          Step-by-step explanation
          1. Header comment and document structure. The comment states the task and the assumed attack rates. <!DOCTYPE html>, <html>, <head> and <body> are the standard skeleton of any web page; meta charset="utf-8" fixes the character encoding.
          2. Style sheet. The CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) rules set the font, the table borders, the teal bar and the colour of each verdict, so the result is readable at a glance.
          3. Table and note. The table is created with its header row only; the rows are added by the script. The note under the table reminds the reader that the figures assume random secrets.
          4. Constants. RATE holds the four assumed speeds (10, 1010, 104 and 1012 guesses per second); YEAR is 31,557,600 seconds.
          5. The list of cases. Each object in ROWS describes one secret (alphabet size and length) attacked in one scenario. An AES-128 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit key) key is described as alphabet 2 and length 128, because each of its 128 bits has two possible values.
          6. Functions. keySpace() computes alphabetlength; averageSeconds() divides half of it by the rate; sci() writes large numbers as a × 10b; readable() picks seconds, minutes, hours, days or years; verdict() applies the thresholds of 100 years and 30 days.
          7. The loop. For each case, the script computes space, seconds and the verdict v, creates a table row, fills its six cells (the bar width is log10(seconds) ÷ 70 of the cell), and appends it with appendChild, which makes it appear.
          8. Reading the result. The same 8-letter password moves from Withstands (online, rate-limited) to Does not (stolen fast hash, 10 seconds) to Partly (slow salted hash, about 121 days). A 15-letter password reaches about 2,700 years even behind a fast hash, and a 4-word passphrase about 5,800 years behind a slow hash; random AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) keys are beyond any physical possibility.

          Practice Check your understanding: 4 MCQs (Multiple-Choice Questions) and 2 MSQs (Multiple-Select Questions)
          

          In-class practice only; these questions are not quiz Q_03. Answer, use the hint if needed, then reveal the answer and the explanation of every option. 
          

          MCQ Question 1 · multiple-choice 1 of 4 · one answer
          An attacker tries the password Winter2026! against all 300 accounts of a company, then waits one hour before trying Summer2026! against all of them again. What is this attack called?
          Hint: Few passwords, many accounts, slow pace to stay under the lockout threshold.
          MCQ Question 2 · multiple-choice 2 of 4 · one answer
          Which measure directly defends a web server against downgrade attacks?
          Hint: A downgrade forces an older version. What if the older version is not available at all?
          MCQ Question 3 · multiple-choice 3 of 4 · one answer
          Code 4 estimates about 5.4 × 1018 years to brute-force a random AES-128 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 128-bit key) key at 1012 keys per second. What is the correct conclusion for a defender?
          Hint: If the key itself cannot be searched, where will an attacker look instead?
          MCQ Question 4 · multiple-choice 4 of 4 · one answer
          What did the SHAttered research (2017) demonstrate?
          Hint: It concerns a hash function that was still widely used at the time.
          MSQ Question 5 · multiple-select 1 of 2 · several answers
          Which measures reduce the success of ONLINE password guessing against NorthMaple's VPN (Virtual Private Network) portal? (Select 4)
          Hint: Online means the attacker must go through the live login service, which the defender controls.
          MSQ Question 6 · multiple-select 2 of 2 · several answers
          Which statements about on-path (man-in-the-middle) attacks and their defenses are correct? (Select 3)
          Hint: Encryption helps only if you know who holds the other end of the key exchange.

          Work on your own lab machine NM-LX01 (Linux) or NM-WS01 (Windows). Record every command and its output; this becomes the first draft of the validation section of Chapter 6.
          

            

          1. Create a small test file: echo "NorthMaple lab file - Class 14" > nm_test.txt
            2. 

          2. Hash it with OpenSSL: openssl dgst -sha256 nm_test.txt. On Linux, sha256sum nm_test.txt gives the same value. On Windows PowerShell: Get-FileHash .\nm_test.txt -Algorithm SHA256 (SHA-256 (Secure Hash Algorithm, 256-bit output) is the default of this cmdlet) https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/microsoft.powershell.utility/get-filehash.
            3. 

          3. Change one character in the file (14 becomes 15) and hash it again. Compare the two digests: nothing in the second one resembles the first (avalanche effect).
            4. 

          4. Hash a lab-only password twice with a random salt: openssl passwd -6 'Lab-Only-Passw0rd'. The two results differ, because each run draws a new salt https://docs.openssl.org/master/man1/openssl-passwd/.
            5. 

          5. Hash it twice with a fixed salt: openssl passwd -6 -salt NMlab2026 'Lab-Only-Passw0rd'. The two results are identical. Explain in one sentence why.
            6. 

          6. Write the four digests and your explanation in your Course Procedure Manual draft.
            7.

          LAB_06 at a glance (the full lab brief is distributed separately)
          Slide 54LAB_06 at a glance, and next steps
          

          LAB_06, VPN (Virtual Private Network) Setup and Encryption Configuration, runs over Classes 16 and 17 and is worth 5 %. In part 1 you set up a remote-access VPN into the NorthMaple network (WireGuard recommended; alternatives accepted) and connect the remote-worker client through it. In part 2 you encrypt one folder or volume of company data with a free tool, enable HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure) with a self-signed certificate on one internal service, and validate both: the VPN traffic is encrypted and the service answers only over HTTPS. The deliverable (VPN configuration, encryption steps and validation evidence) becomes Chapter 6 of the Final Project and of the Course Procedure Manual.

          Appendix A
          Glossary
          

          

          

          Every term printed in teal bold in the lessons, with its definition. Type to filter.
          TermDefinitionLesson
          /etc/shadowThe Linux file, readable only by root, that stores password hashes in the format $id$salt$hash.Lesson 2
          AEAD (Authenticated Encryption with Associated Data) / authentication tagAn encryption mode that provides confidentiality and integrity; the tag detects any modification of the ciphertext.Lesson 1
          Asymmetric encryptionTwo linked keys: the public key is shared, the private key is kept secret (RSA (Rivest–Shamir–Adleman), ECC (Elliptic Curve Cryptography)).Lesson 1
          Avalanche effectA one-bit change in the input changes about half of the output bits.Lesson 1
          Brute-force attackTrying every possible key or password; average time = half the key space divided by the guess rate.Lesson 4
          Collision / birthday attackFinding two inputs with the same hash; generic cost about 2^(n/2) for an n-bit hash.Lesson 4
          Collision resistanceIt is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest.Lesson 1
          Constant-time comparisonA comparison that always takes the same time, so response time reveals nothing about the stored value.Lesson 2
          CryptanalysisThe study of methods for defeating cryptographic protection.Lesson 4
          Crypto-agilityThe ability to replace cryptographic algorithms without rebuilding systems.Lesson 4
          Crypto-eraseMaking encrypted data permanently unreadable by destroying every copy of its key.Lesson 3
          CryptographyThe science of protecting information with mathematical algorithms so that only authorized parties can read it and so that modification or false origin can be detected.Lesson 1
          Data at rest / in transit / in useStored data; data moving across a network; data being processed in memory by the CPU (Central Processing Unit).Lesson 3
          Dictionary / rule-based attackTrying words from lists of real passwords, with the predictable modifications people apply.Lesson 4
          Diffie-Hellman key exchangeA method for two parties to compute the same shared secret over an open network without sending it.Lesson 1
          Digital signatureA value computed from a document's hash with the signer's private key; anyone verifies it with the public key.Lesson 1
          Downgrade attackForcing the negotiation of an older protocol or weaker cipher; defeated by disabling old versions.Lesson 4
          EavesdroppingPassive capture of network traffic to read its content (MITRE ATT&CK (Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge) T1040).Lesson 3
          Enrollment / verificationEnrollment stores the hash of a new password; verification hashes the typed password with the same method and compares.Lesson 2
          File or container encryptionEncryption of selected files or an encrypted container (EFS (Encrypting File System), VeraCrypt, 7-Zip AES-256 (Advanced Encryption Standard, 256-bit key), GnuPG); for containers and encrypted archives the protection travels with the copied file.Lesson 3
          Forward secrecySession keys come from ephemeral key exchanges, so a later theft of the server's long-term private key does not decrypt recorded sessions.Lesson 3
          Full-disk encryptionEncryption of a whole volume (BitLocker, LUKS (Linux Unified Key Setup), FileVault); protects a powered-off or hibernated device, not a running system, even with the screen locked.Lesson 3
          Harvest now, decrypt later / post-quantum cryptographyRecording traffic today to decrypt it with a future quantum computer; answered by new algorithms such as ML-KEM (FIPS (Federal Information Processing Standards) 203).Lesson 4
          Hash function / digestA one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size output; no key, not reversible.Lesson 1
          HMAC (Hash-based Message Authentication Code)A hash computed with a secret key; proves integrity and origin.Lesson 1
          Hybrid encryption / session keyAsymmetric cryptography establishes a random symmetric session key; symmetric encryption protects the data.Lesson 1
          Kerckhoffs's principleA cryptosystem must stay secure even if everything except the key is public; use published, standardized algorithms.Lesson 1
          Key / key length / key spaceThe secret value used by an algorithm; its size in bits; the set of all possible keys (2 to the power of the key length).Lesson 1
          Key managementGeneration, storage, backup, rotation, revocation and destruction of keys; the key must be stored apart from the data.Lesson 3
          Key stretching / work factorMaking each hash deliberately expensive (iterations, cost, memory) so that each guess costs the attacker time.Lesson 2
          Link vs end-to-end encryptionLink encryption protects one segment and is removed at each device; end-to-end encryption protects data from sender to final receiver.Lesson 3
          Lookup table / rainbow tablePrecomputed tables that map hashes back to passwords; a rainbow table stores chains to save space. Both fail against salted hashes.Lesson 2
          Memory-hard functionA password-hashing function that needs a large amount of RAM (Random-Access Memory) per guess (scrypt, Argon2id, yescrypt), which limits parallel cracking on GPUs (Graphics Processing Units).Lesson 2
          Mode of operationThe rule that applies a block cipher to data longer than one block (ECB (Electronic Codebook), CBC (Cipher Block Chaining), GCM (Galois/Counter Mode), XTS (XEX-based Tweaked-codebook mode with ciphertext Stealing)).Lesson 1
          NonceA number used only once with a given key; reuse with GCM (Galois/Counter Mode) leaks information about the plaintexts and allows forged authentication tags.Lesson 1
          NT (New Technology) hashThe Windows password hash: MD4 (Message Digest 4) of the password, not salted.Lesson 2
          On-path (man-in-the-middle) attackAn attacker relays and can read or alter traffic between two parties; defeated by authenticated key exchange and certificate validation.Lesson 4
          Online vs offline attackGuessing against a live login (rate-limited, logged) versus guessing against stolen hashes on the attacker's own hardware.Lesson 4
          Password spraying / credential stuffingOne common password against many accounts; stolen username-password pairs replayed on other services.Lesson 4
          PepperA secret value added to all passwords and stored outside the database.Lesson 2
          Plaintext / ciphertextPlaintext is readable data; ciphertext is the unreadable result of encryption.Lesson 1
          Replay attackResending a captured valid message; defeated by nonces, timestamps and counters.Lesson 4
          SaltA unique random value per password, combined with it before hashing and stored in clear; defeats precomputed tables and hides password reuse.Lesson 2
          Side-channel attackExtracting secrets from time, power, emissions or cache behaviour of a computation; defeated by constant-time implementations.Lesson 4
          Steganography / LSB (Least Significant Bit) substitutionHiding the existence of a message inside a cover file, for example in the least significant bits of pixel values.Lesson 1
          Symmetric encryptionOne shared secret key both encrypts and decrypts (AES (Advanced Encryption Standard), ChaCha20). Fast; the key must be distributed securely.Lesson 1
          TLS (Transport Layer Security) handshakeThe first phase of TLS (Transport Layer Security): version and cipher-suite negotiation, ephemeral key exchange, server authentication by certificate, derivation of session keys.Lesson 3

          Legal Notice, Disclaimer, and Acceptable Use Policy — Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) — Cybersecurity AEC (Attestation d'études collégiales), LEA.D8 — Competency EZ03: To apply access control measures.
          
Author and owner: Cyber.SoHo · Version 1.0 · Effective date: August 29, 2026 · Applies to every lecture, lab, project, quiz, exam, document, video, and social-media publication of the course, including this page.
          

          1. Plain-Language Summary
          

          This document protects everyone: the students, the viewers, and the author. In short: all the material of this course is provided for education only. You may practice the activities only inside your own, isolated laboratory environment, or on systems for which you hold explicit written permission. You are fully and solely responsible for your own actions, your equipment, your accounts, your costs, and your time. By reading, watching, downloading, or using any part of the material, you accept this entire document.
          

          2. Educational Purpose Only
          

          All lectures, labs, projects, quizzes, exams, documents, videos, and social-media publications of the course Cyber Defense (420-D03-AB) (together, "the Material") are created for one purpose: teaching defensive cybersecurity to adult learners of the Cybersecurity AEC (Attestation d'études collégiales) program. The Material shows how to protect systems, not how to attack the systems of others. Nothing in the Material is an invitation, an instruction, or an authorization to access, test, or damage any real system, network, account, or data.
          

          3. Acceptable Use and Prohibited Actions (Student Warning)
          

          You may:
          • Practice only inside your personal, isolated laboratory environment, as defined in LAB_01: a local virtualization tool (for example VirtualBox) or your own personal free-tier cloud account on AWS (Amazon Web Services) or Microsoft Azure.
          • Practice on any other system only if you hold explicit written permission from the owner of that system, obtained before you start.
          • Use snapshots and isolated virtual networks so that a mistake stays inside your laboratory.
          

          You must never:
          • Scan, probe, attack, intercept, monitor, or access any system, network, wireless network, or account that is not yours, including those of the college, an employer, a business, a public website, or a neighbor.
          • Create, install, or release malicious software outside your isolated laboratory.
          • Attempt password, credential, or interception attacks against any real account or any real communication.
          • Use the Material, or any tool presented in it, to break any law or any policy that applies to you.
          

          Cloud responsibilities: If you use a cloud account, you must respect the acceptable-use policies of the provider (AWS (Amazon Web Services) or Microsoft Azure). Free tiers have limits; monitor them. All cloud costs, overage charges, and account consequences are your responsibility.
          

          4. Legal Warning
          

          Unauthorized computer access or use is a criminal offence. In Canada, the Criminal Code contains, among other provisions: section 342.1 (unauthorized use of a computer) https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-46/section-342.1.html, section 342.2 (possession of a device to obtain unauthorized use of a computer) https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-46/section-342.2.html, and section 430(1.1) (mischief in relation to computer data) https://laws-lois.justice.gc.ca/eng/acts/C-46/section-430.html. Penalties can include imprisonment. If you are located outside Canada, the laws of your own country, province, or state apply to you, and you must know and obey them. The policies and codes of conduct of your college apply in addition to the law. The instructor never asks for, and never authorizes, any illegal act. If an activity seems to touch a system you do not own, stop and ask the instructor before doing anything.
          

          5. Assumption of Risk and Limitation of Liability
          

          You use the Material at your own risk, on your own or rented equipment, and on your own or class time. To the maximum extent permitted by law, Cyber.SoHo and the instructor — in every role: teacher, author, instructor, researcher, and publisher on social platforms — are not responsible for any direct or indirect damage, data loss, hardware or software failure, service or account suspension, financial cost, or legal consequence resulting from the use or the misuse of the Material, by you or by anyone else.

          11. Ethics and Responsible Conduct
          

          The course teaches defensive ("white-hat") cybersecurity. By using the Material, students agree to use their skills only to protect, never to harm, and to respect the privacy of others. If a student accidentally discovers a real vulnerability, the student reports it responsibly to the owner of the system and to the instructor, instead of exploiting it or publishing it. Academic integrity applies at all times, including the course rule on AI (Artificial Intelligence): any use of an AI tool in a submission must state the LLM (Large Language Model) used and the exact prompt(s) given to it.
          

          In practice: the model drafts, the analyst decides, and the analyst's name goes on the record. Never paste real keys, hashes, passwords or client data into an online AI (Artificial Intelligence) service; when an assistant must see lab material, use a local model bound to 127.0.0.1 (for example Ollama).
